blocks.text: Re: Reserve adequacy review
Dear Michelle:

Thank you for the time you and your colleagues gave us while we worked out the shape of this review. This letter puts what we agreed in writing. It says what we will do, what we will rely on, who will do the work, and the terms we will work under. We have kept it plain, because it is the document both of us will go back to if a question about the work comes up later.
What we have been asked to do

{{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}} has asked us to review the reserves it carries and to give an opinion on whether they are adequate as of a valuation date we will settle with you at the outset. The opinion is the product. Everything else we do is there to support it. The review has four parts.
1. We will reconcile the reserve data you provide to your own financial records, so that the figures we test are the figures you carry.
2. We will review the methods and assumptions behind the current reserves, and set out which of them are prescribed and which rest on judgment.
3. We will develop our own estimate of the reserves required, from the reconciled data and from assumptions we are prepared to support.
4. We will compare our estimate with the carried reserves, explain any difference by its source, and state our opinion in a written report.

Work not on that list is outside this engagement. We are not auditing your financial statements, and we are not setting your reserves for you. If either becomes useful, we can scope it separately and in writing.
How we will go about it

We start with the data, because an opinion can be no better than the records under it. The first weeks go to assembling your files and checking them. We will send one itemized request rather than a series of small ones. What we will need falls into three groups.
1. The reserve detail as of the valuation date, at whatever level your systems hold it.
2. The year-end financial records in which those reserves are reported.
3. The documentation for the methods and assumptions in use at the valuation date, including any change made during the year and the reason for it.

We will rely on the data you give us. We will test it for internal consistency and reconcile it to your records, but we will not audit it. Where we find a gap, we will ask about it. Where a question cannot be answered, we will say in writing what we assumed in its place, and we will carry that assumption into the report where you can see it.

The work will be performed under the Actuarial Standards of Practice that apply to it, among them ASOP No. 23, Data Quality, and ASOP No. 41, Actuarial Communications. Our report will keep three things apart: what the data show, what we assumed, and what we conclude. Where a conclusion depends on an assumption, the report will say so in a paragraph of its own, so that anyone who reads it can see what the conclusion rests on.
Who will do the work

Jennifer Vasquez, a Consulting Actuary with our firm, will lead the review from day to day. She is your first call on scope, schedule, and any question of judgment. David Sherman, a Senior Analyst, will build the reserve model and carry out the reconciliation. Megan Dudley, an Actuarial Associate, will handle most of the correspondence with your staff about files and records, and she will keep the log of what we have asked for and what has arrived. I will review the work at each stage, and I will sign the opinion.

Requests for data go astray when several people on each side are asking and answering. We would like you to be our point of contact for data, with Megan Dudley as ours, so that one person on each side knows what has been asked for and what is still open, and your staff are not answering the same question twice.
Timing and fee

We expect to begin work on {{fact:f:E-2017-001.start}} and to need about seven months from that date to the final report. Most of the risk to that schedule sits in the data. If the files arrive complete, the schedule holds. If they do not, we will tell you promptly what has moved and why.
Our fee for the work described in this letter is a fixed fee of {{fact:f:E-2017-001.fee}}.
Fees and payment

The fixed fee covers the reconciliation, the review of methods and assumptions, our estimate, a draft report, one round of questions on the draft, and the final report. We will invoice it in three parts: at the start of the work, on delivery of the draft, and on delivery of the final report. Invoices are payable within thirty days. If you ask us for work outside the scope above, we will agree on a fee for it with you in writing before we begin.
Term and termination

This engagement runs from the start of the work until we deliver the final report. Either of us may end it by written notice to the other. If it ends early, you will owe us for the work done up to the date of the notice and for nothing after it. We will then return or destroy your data, as you direct, apart from what our working papers are required to keep.
Confidentiality

We will hold the information you give us in confidence and use it only for this engagement. We will not disclose it outside our firm unless you agree in writing or the law requires it. If the law requires it, we will tell you first unless we are prevented from doing so. Our working papers are held under the same duty.
Limitation of liability

Our report is prepared for {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}} and for the purpose stated in it. No one else may rely on it without our written consent. Our total liability arising out of this engagement, in contract or otherwise, is limited to the fees you have paid us under this letter, except where the law does not permit such a limit.
Governing law
This letter and the engagement it describes are governed by the laws of the state in which our office is located.

If these terms match your understanding, please sign below on behalf of {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}} and return a signed copy to me. We will begin once we have it. If anything here reads differently from what we discussed, call me before you sign and we will correct the wording. We are glad to be doing this work with you and your team.
Sincerely,

Now that the engagement letter is signed and the work has formally begun as of {{fact:f:E-2017-001.start}}, I wanted to set down in one place what we have promised {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}} and how we have agreed to share the work, so that we are all starting from the same picture. What the client has engaged us for is a single opinion: whether the reserves it carries are adequate as of the valuation date we settle with Michelle Hudson and her team. All of the work between now and the report is in service of that opinion, and the report will keep what the data show, what we assumed, and what we conclude in separate places. That is much easier to do at the end if we keep them separate in our own files from the first week.
Who is carrying what

David Sherman will build the reserve model, load each file as it arrives, and tie the reserve detail to the year-end financial records. Because he will see every file first, he is usually going to be the one who finds a problem in the data before the rest of us do, so a question about what a file contains should go to him before it goes anywhere else.

Jennifer Johnson is joining us to work with David on the reconciliation, which is the part of this review the opinion leans on most. She will take the comparison of the reserve detail with the prior year's figures, and she will keep a running note of every point where something had to be assumed to make the figures agree, along with the provision or standard behind each choice. Those notes will become the backbone of the data section of the report, so it is worth writing them as if someone outside the team will read them.

Jennifer Vasquez leads the review day to day and will take the assumption work herself: which of the client's assumptions are prescribed, which rest on judgment, and which of that second group we are prepared to support. She will review every exhibit before it leaves the office, and anything she cannot trace back to a source will come back to whoever built it.

I will handle the correspondence with the client's staff, keep the request log, and draft the data section. Michelle Hudson, their Director of Operations, is our point of contact for everything to do with data, and the letter told her that requests would reach her through one person on our side. I would ask that questions for her team come through me, even the small ones, so that she is not hearing from four of us at once and we always know what is still open.
The first weeks

Almost all of the early work is about data. The itemized request goes out first. Once files begin to arrive, David Sherman loads them and he and Jennifer Johnson begin the reconciliation, while I log each one against the request and write back to Michelle Hudson about anything missing or inconsistent, with a note of what we will assume if a correction does not come back. Jennifer Vasquez can start on the assumption documentation as soon as it is in hand, since that piece does not need to wait for the reconciliation.

None of this will produce a number anyone outside the team sees for some weeks yet, which is what we want at this stage. If something in the first files looks as though it could change the shape of the work, please say so early, and we will take it to Jennifer Vasquez together.
I will send round a draft of the data request tomorrow. The one thing I need from each of you is your comments on it by the middle of next week, so that it can go to Michelle Hudson in one piece.
Hello Michelle,

Thank you for the first set of files for the {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}} reserve adequacy review. They came through last week, and David has now loaded both the reserve detail and the year-end figures, so this seemed the right moment to start a single thread for our questions about the data. Jennifer and David are copied, so whoever on our side is closest to a question can pick it up.

For the most part the two agree well, but there is one thing we would like your team's help with. A small group of records appears twice in the reserve detail, with the same identifiers and the same reserve amounts, and the only difference between the two copies is the date the extract was run. Our best guess is that the extract was run twice and both runs ended up in the file, in which case each pair is really one record and the detail, as it stands, counts those reserves twice.

If we do not hear otherwise, we will treat each pair as a single record, keep one copy, and note that in our working papers as an assumption we made rather than something the data told us. We would much prefer to know for certain, though, since it affects the figure we reconcile to. What we need next is a word from whoever runs the extract on whether it was run more than once.
Best,
Good morning Michelle,

The duplicates Megan described account for the difference between the reserve detail and your year-end figure. With the second copy of each pair set aside, the two agree within rounding. That result is preliminary until your team confirms how the extract was run.
The steps, so that your staff can check them:

1. I totaled the reserve detail as received and compared it with the year-end figure in your financial records. The detail was higher.
2. I matched records on identifier and reserve amount. Every pair matched on both and differed only in the extract date.
3. With one copy of each pair removed, the remaining difference is within rounding.

I have entered the adjusted file in our data log for {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}} as provisional and used it for this check only. Nothing from it goes into the reserve model until the double run is confirmed.
Best,
Hello Michelle,

One small addition to David's note, so that you have the choice in front of you. If confirming how the extract was run means someone has to dig back through the job history, a fresh extract taken once, as of the same valuation date, would settle the question just as well and may be quicker for your team. Either one gives us what we need.

In the meantime nothing on our side is held up. We will carry on with the parts of the {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}} review that do not depend on these records, and the reconciliation will stay where David has it until we hear from you. The one thing we need next is either the confirmation or the fresh extract, whichever is easier at your end.
Best,
Good morning Michelle,
The fresh extract your team sent today resolves the question. Each record now appears once, and the reserve detail agrees with your year-end figure within rounding, with no adjustment on our part.
For the record of the reconciliation:

1. I loaded the new extract in place of the original and totaled it against the year-end figure in your financial records.
2. I compared it with the original file record by record. The only records absent from the new extract are the second copies of the pairs Megan described.
3. I have set the original file aside and recorded the replacement, and the reason for it, in our data log.

This is a reconciliation of totals and record counts. It does not yet test the individual fields the model draws on, which is the next step, and it says nothing yet about whether the reserves {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}} carries are adequate.
Best,
